la:verb:promulgo.html:
prōmulgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
etym. unknown
, in publicist's lang.,
Lit., to expose to public view (as a proposed new law, etc.), to make known, publish, promulgate (cf.: edico, pronuntio): promulgari leges dicuntur, cum primum in vulgus eduntur, quasi provulgari, Paul. ex Müll.: leges cum quae latae sunt, tum quae promulgatae fuerunt,: legem,: leges,; ; ; ; : rogationem,; ; : res multos dies promulgata et cognita,: proelia,: dies fastos,.—
Transf., in gen., to make known, to teach (very rare): majores oculorum medicamentis aconitum misceri saluberrime promulgavere,.

la:noun:promissor.html:
prōmissor, ōris, m.
id.
,
a promiser, esp. who promises great things (very rare), Hor A. P 138; Zumpt.

la:verb:promitto.html:
prō-mitto, mīsi, missum, 3 (sync. forms:
promisti for promisisti,; : promisse for promisisse,: promissem,; archaic inf. pass. promittier, ), v. a.
Lit., to let go forward, to send or put forth, to let hang down, let grow, etc. (rare; not in Cic.): ramos vel ferro compescunt vel longius promittunt,suffer to grow longer,.—Reflex., to grow: nec ulla arborum avidius se promittit,.—Of the hair, the beard, to let hang down, let grow: satis constat multos mortales capillum ac barbam promisisse,; ; cf.: pogoniae, quibus inferiore ex parte promittitur juba,.—Transf.: (Sonus lusciniae) promittitur revocato spiritu,is drawn out, prolonged,; Gallia est longe et a nostris litoribus huc usque promissa,; v.infra, P. a.—
Trop., of speech.
To say beforehand, to forebode, foretell, predict, prophesy (very rare): praesertim cum, si mihi alterum utrum de eventu rerum promittendum esset, id futurum, quod evenit, exploratius possem promittere,: ut (di) primis minentur extis, bene promittant secundis,.—Of signs or omens, to forebode, portend: pari in meliora praesagio in Caesaris castris omnia aves victimaeque promiserant,: promittunt omina poenas,: clarum fore (Servium) visa circa caput flamma promiserat, Flor 1, 6, 1; 1, 7, 9.—Also, in gen., to denote beforehand: stella ... vindemiae maturitatem promittens,.—
To promise, hold out, cause to expect, give hope or promise of, assure (class. and freq.; syn.: polliceor, spondeo, recipio), constr. with acc., an object-clause, or de: domum,: sestertia septem,: carmen,, dona, Ov Tr. 4, 2, 7: auxilium alicui,: opem,: salutem,: ea quae tibi promitto ac recipio,: si Neptunus quod Theseo promiserat, non fecisset,: dii faxint, ut faciat ea quae promittit!.— With inf. (usu. fut. inf.): promitto, recipio, spondeo, C. Caesarem talem semper fore civem, qualis hodie sit,; cf.: promitto, in meque recipio fore eum, etc.,: quem inimicissimum futurum esse promitto et spondeo,: surrepturum pallam promisit tibi,; ; cf. : promisit Apollo Ambiguam tellure novā Salamina futuram,; .—With inf. pres.: si operam dare promittitis,; ; : magorum vanitas ebrietati eas resistere

promittit, ; cf.: se remedium afferer tantamque vim morbi levaturum esse promisit, monstrare, : promittere oratorem,to give promise of becoming,; cf.: per ea scelera se parricidam,excite fears lest he become,: me Promisi ultorem,.—With de: de alicujus voluntate promittere,: de me tibi sic promitto atque confirmo, me, etc.,; : promittere damni infecti,i. e. to promise indemnification for, become answerable for the possible damage,.—

With ut and subj.: promiserat ut daret,.—Of things' terra ipsa promittit (aquas), gives promise of, leads one to expect water, : debet extremitas (picturae) sic desinere, ut promittat alia post se,to lead one to suppose, to suggest,; .—
In partic.
To promise to come, to engage one's self to meet any one, to dine, sup, etc., ; : ad fratrem,: ad cenam mihi,; ; so, tibi me promittere noli,to expect me,.—
To promise something to a deity, i. e. to vow: donum Jovi dicatum atque promissum,: nigras pecudes Diti,; Juv 13, 233; Petr 88; .—
To offer as a price (post-Aug.): pro domo sestertium millies promittens,. 1, 1, § 3. —Hence, prōmissus, a, um, P a.
Lit., hanging down, long; of the hair: coma, Varr. ap. ; ; : Britanni capillo sunt promisso,; so, capillus,: barba,; : barba omnibus promissa erat,; ; .—Of the dewlap: boves palearibus amplis et paene ad genua promissis,.—Of the belly: sues ventre promisso,.—
Subst.: prōmissum, i, n., a promise (very freq. in prose and poetry; cf. promissio, pollicitatio),: voto quodam et promisso teneri,: constantia promissi,: promissum absolvere,: facere,; : exigere,: ludere aliquem promisso inani,.—In plur.: pacta et promissa servare,: illis promissis standum non est, quae, etc.,: promissis manere,: promissa firmare,: multa fidem promissa levant,: dic aliquid dignum promissis,: quo promissa (Ennii) cadant,i. e. the expectations which he raises,: promissa dare,to make promises,; to fulfil, .

la:noun:promulsis.html:
prō-mulsis, ĭdis, f.
mulsum
.
Lit., a relish of eggs, salt fish, mead, etc., servedfirst at a Roman banquet, a whet, antepast, ; .—
Transf.
A foretaste: libidinis,—
For promulsidare, the tray for the antepast, .

la:verb:promereo.gloss: to be deserving of, deserve, merit, earn
senses: to be deserving of, deserve, merit, earn
to acquire, earn, gain, get, win
la:verb:promereo.html:
prō-mĕrĕo, ŭi, ĭtum, 2, v. a., and prō-mĕrĕor, ĭtus, 2,
v. dep. a.
To deserve, be deserving of, merit, in a good or bad sense (class.)
In gen.: retineri nequeo, quin dicam ea, quae promeres,; : quid mali sum promeritus,: ita velim me promerentem ames,: reus levius punitus quam sit ille promeritus,: poenam,.—In a good sense: promeruisti, ut ne quid ores, quin impetres,: promerenti optime hoccine pretii redditur,; deorum indulgentiam,: amorem,: omnium voluntatem, dies qui primus videre Promeruit nasci mundum, .—
Esp., to deserve of one any thing (good or bad); constr. usu. with de or absol., rarely with acc.: numquam referre gratiam possum satis, proinde ut tu promeritus de me,: paratiores erunt ad bene de multis promerendum,.—
Transf., to acquire, gain, earn, get, win homines tenues unum habent in nostrum ordinem aut promerendi aut proferendi beneficii losum, socios, : principem,: ego te numquam negabo Promeritam,: per hostias deos laevos,i. e. to render favorable, to propitiate,; cf. pass.: talibus enim hostiis promeretur Deus,is won, conciliated,.—Hence, prō-mĕrĭtum, i, n, desert (good or evil), merit.—In good sense, Pac. ap. (Trag. Rel. p. 79 Rib.); Lucr 2, 651; ; .—In bad sense, ; Auct. B. Afr. 90.
la:verb:promereo.inflection: ŭi, ĭtum, 2, v. a., ĭtus, 2, v. dep. a.

la:verb:promo.gloss: to take or bring out or forth, produce, bring to light
senses: to take or bring out or forth, produce, bring to light
la:verb:promo.html:
prōmo, mpsi (msi), mptum (mtum), 3, v. a.
pro-emo
,
to take, give, or bring out or forth, to produce (freq. and class.; syn.: profero, effero)
Lit.: si quid tibi opus erit promptu, promito,: Pa. Prompsisti tu illi vinum? Lu. Non prompsi, : pecuniam ex aerario,: signa ex aerario prompta,: medicamenta de narthecio,: aurum ex armario,: libros inde,: vina dolio,: promptum vagina pugionem, aliquid in usus, : se, to come forth or out: laetique cavo se robore promunt,: vites promunt se,put forth, shoot out,.—
Trop.
In gen., to bring, put, or draw forth est aliquid, quod non ex usu forensi...sit promendum et assumendum, : loci, e quibus argumenta promuntur,: nunc promenda tibi sunt consilia,: promere et exercere justitiam,: nunc illas promite vires,.—
In partic., to bring to light, disclose, utter, tell, express, relate, etc.: percuntanti promere omnia. : rerum ordinem,: magnificam orationem de semet ipso prompsit,. verba, quae sensum animi nostri optime promunt, : animi voluntatem,: promere aliquid loquendo, : quid ipse sim secutus promam,: qui pueris utile carmen prompturus est, wishes to publish, p 358 med.; cf.: insignem attenuat deus, Obscura promens,raising into notice,.—Hence, promp-tus (promtus), a, um, P. a., prop. brought to light, exposed to view; hence,
Visible, apparent, evident, manifest (rare but class.): inimicitiam atque amicitiam in frontem promptam gero, Enn. ap. (Trag. v 8 Vahl.): aliud clausum in pectore, aliud promptum in linguā habere,: tametsi hoc minime latet, quod ita promptum et propositum est, ut, etc., prompta et aperta, : eminentia et prompta,: consilia, locos, prompta, occulta noverat,.—Sup.: nihil se tam clausum neque tam reconditum posse habere, quod non istius cupiditati apertissimum promptissimumque esset,.—
Transf.
At hand, i. e. prepared, ready, quick, prompt, inclined or disposed to or for any thing = paratus, expeditus.
Absol.: laudat promptos, segniores castigat,: promptissimus homo,: cetera, quae tibi a multis prompta esse certo scio, a me sunt paratissima,: fidem alicui promptam expositamque praebere,: quorum cognoverat promptam audaciam,: quod cuique promptum, arma, equos, aurum offerentes,: sagittae,: prompta et profluens eloquentia,.—Sup., .—
With ad or in aliquid (rarely in aliquū re): ad bella suscipienda Gallorum aiacer et promptus est animus,: animus ad defendendam rem publicam, Cic Fam. 3, 11, 4. esse animo prompto ad jocandum,: homines ad vim prompti, ad seditionem parati,: paratior ad usum forensem promptiorque esse,: promptiores ad nostra pericula,: promptus ad lacessendum certamen, Liv 44, 4, 2: ad injurias vicinorum,: promptus in pavorem,: in adulationes,: in latrocinia, Flor 4, 12, 10; cf. in comp.: promptior in spem,; and in sup.: Dalmatae in latrocinia promptissimi, Flor 4, 12, 10: celeritas prompta et parata in agendo,: in rebus gerendis promptus,.—
With pro or adversus (very rare): utemini nobis etiam promptioribus pro patriā,: promptus adversus insontes,—
With abl.: non promptus ingenio,: linguā promptus,; cf.: sermone promptus,: promptus audaciā,; : promptus animo,.—Comp.: haud quisquam manu promptior erat,: promptior linguā quam manu,.—(ε) With gen.: promptus animi,.—Sup.: belli promptissimos delegebant, ap. Arus Mess. (H. 2, 13 Dietsch): Plato veritatis omnibus exhibendae promptissimus,.—(ζ) With dat. (rare except in Tacitus): promptus libertati aut ad mortem animus,: seditioni,: cuicumque fiagitio,: ultioni,: nullam gentem promptiorem veniae dandae fuisse,. —(η) With inf. (poet.): promptus metuenda pati,: scis ipse, quam promptae superos incessere Thebae,.—
In gen., brave, courageous: maxime vellem, rem publicam in periculis a promptissumo quoque defendi, Sall. Or. Phil. cont. Lep. (H. 1, 48 Dietsch); ; ; .—
Easy, practicable: facilis et prompta defensio,: moenia haudquaquam prompta oppugnanti,: regnum,: expugnatio,: possessio,: aditus, obvia comitas,fin.: promptissima mortis via,: promptum est, with inf., it is easy: sed nec mihi dicere promptum, Nec facere est illi, Ov M. 13, 10; .—Hence, adv.: promptē (perh. not ante-Aug.).
Readily, quickly, without delay, willingly, promptly: dare operam,: distribuere pecuniam legatis, .—Comp.: promptius adversari,: dirumpere imagines (opp. cunctanter),.— Sup.: promptissime adesse alicui,.—
Easily: promptius expediam,: victoria promptissime licentiam sumministrat,.

la:verb:promoveo.gloss: to move forward, cause to advance, push onward, propel, advance
senses: to move forward, cause to advance, push onward, propel, advance
to bring to pass, effect, accomplish, progress
la:verb:promoveo.html:
prō-mōvĕo, mōvi, mōtum (
pluperf. promorat. Hor Epod. 11, 14: promosset, Jahn), 2, v. a., to move forward, cause to advance, push onward, advance.
Lit.
In gen.: saxa vectibus, Caes B. C. 2, 11: onera,; : assa in alterum apodyterii anguium,: legiones,: castra ad Carthaginem, to move onward, Liv 28, 44 fin.: exercitu in Aetoliam promoto,: cornua utrimque (in acie),: scalas et machinamenta,: calculum,to push forward, move,; : unum pedem triclinio,to put forth, move from,: ibi te videbo et promovebo,will take you along with me, —
In partic., to extend, enlarge. moenia Ostia tenus, Suet Ner 16: imperium, Ov P 2, 2, 72: vires in immensum orbem,.—
Med. t. t., to put out of joint, dislocate, displace: in palmā quoque ossa interdum suis sedibus promoventur,: femur in omnes quattuor partes promovetur, saepissime in interiorem,—
Trop.
In gen., to bring to pass, effect, accomplish (ante- and post-class.): promovere parum,: aliquis dicat, Nihil promoveris,: meditatio nihil ad vitam tuendam promovens,; cf. in a lusus verbb. with movere se,.—Absol.: cum in studio facundiae abunde promovisset,.—
In partic.
To enlarge, increase: doctrina vim promovet insitam, Hor C. 4, 4, 33; so, promovere aliquem, to advance, prefer, promote (post-Aug.; cf.: perduco, produco, proveho): vetus miles ad eum gradum promotus,: promotus ad amplissimas procurationes,; ; ; ; ; ; .—
To bring to light, reveal: arcana promorat loco (i. e. ex intimo corde), Hor Epod. 11, 14.—
To put off, defer, postpone: nuptias alicui,.—Hence, prōmōtus, a, um, P a.
Of time, advanced, i. e. late: nocte promotā,late at night, far into the night,; , p. 190, 30.—
Subst.: prōmōta, ōrum, n., in the lang. of the Stoics, things that are to be preferred, pref. erable things, as being next in degree to absolute good; a literal transl. of the Gr. προηγμέυα, .

la:noun:promptus.html:
promptus (promtus), ūs, m.
promo, prop. a taking forth; hence
,
An exposing to view, a being visible, visibility; only in the phrase in promptu (esse, habere, ponere, etc.), public, open, visible, manifest, before the eyes: ut (decorum) non reconditā quādam ratione cernatur, sed sit in promptu,; so (opp. reconditiora) ; (opp. interiora) : aliquid ponere in promptu (opp. contegere atque abdere),: ingenium in promptu habere,to display,: iram in promptu gerere,: in promptu scrinia Brutus habet,: in promptu gerunt ova,: in promptu est, with a subject-clause, it is clear, plain, evident: omnibus in promptu manifestumque esse videmus, etc.,; ; .—
Readiness; only in the phrase in promptu esse, habere, to be at hand, to have ready: ea dicam, quae mihi sunt in promptu,; : in promptu habere, quantum natura hominis pecudibus antecedat,. —
Ease, facility; only in the phrase in promptu esse, to be easy, : quadrupedes In promptu regere est,: quam quae comprendere dictis In promptu mihi sit,.

la:noun:promissio.html:
prōmissĭo, ōnis f.
promitto
.
In gen., a promising, promise (class. only in sing.; prop. the act of promising; cf. promissum, the thing promised): provinciae,: auxilii,: scelerum,; cf. Don. .—
In partic., rhet. t. t., a promising: tum promissio, si audierint, probaturos,; .

la:other:Prometheus.html:
Prŏmētheus (trisyl.), ĕi and ĕos, m., =Προμηθεύς (the Forethinker),
a son of Iapetus and Clymene, brother of Epimetheus, and father of Deucalion. He formed men of clay, and animated them by means of fire brought from heaven; for which he was fastened to Caucasus, where a vulture, or, as some say, an eagle, fed upon his entrails, until, at last, it was slain by Hercules,; ; ; ; ; ; ; (4, 4, 7); ; ; .—Poet., transf., of a skilful potter, .—Hence,
Prŏmēthēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Prometheus, Promethean: juga,i. e. the Caucasus,; also called rupes,: fibra,of Prometheus,: creta, Col. poët. 10, 59: lutum,: cruor,: manus,.—
Prŏmēthĭădes, ae, m.patron., the son of Prometheus, Deucalion, .

la:adj:promutuus.html:
prō-mūtŭus, a, um, adj.,
paid over beforehand, advanced, loaned: publicanis (imperabatur) insequentis anni vectigal promutuum,was demanded in advance as a loan, (for which before: insequentis anni mutua pecunia,): vectura,prepaid,. —
Subst.: prōmūtŭum, i, n., an advance, loan, .

prōmuntŭrĭum (prōmon-), ĭi, n.
pro-mineo
.

A part of a mountain projecting into the sea, a headland, promontory, ; ; ; ; ; et saep.—As nom. propr.
Promunturium Apollinis, in Africa, near Utica, now Zibib, ; .—

la:adj:promiscuus.gloss: not separate or distinct, mixed; mutual, shared
senses: not separate or distinct, mixed; mutual, shared
la:adj:promiscuus.html:
prō-miscŭus (collat. form prōmis-cŭs, ; ; ; prob. also ante-class.; v. below the adv. promiscam), a, um, adj.
misceo
.
Lit., mixed, not separate or distinct, without distinction, in common, indiscriminate, promiscuous (as adj. not in Cic. or Cæs.): opera promiscua,: conubia, i. e. between patricians and plebeians, Liv 4, 2; cf.: consulatum promiscuum patribus ac plebi facere,. multitudo, of patricians and plebeians, : vulgus,: promiscua omnium generum caedes,: sepultura,: jus,: spectaculum,to which all are admitted without distinction,: divina atque humana promiscua habere,: privatae et promiscuae copiae,common, general, public,: promiscuos feminarum concubitus permittere,. —With object-clause: muta ista et inanima (sc. tecta) intercidere ac reparari promiscua sunt,may be destroyed and restored again,—In neutr. absol.: in promiscuo licentiam atque improbitatem esse voluit,to be universal,; ; : nec arma in promiscuo, sed clausa sub custode,i. e. in every man's hands,.—
In partic., in gram., epicene: promiscuum nomen, i. e. epicoenum,.—
Transf., common, usual (very rare and not ante-Aug.): promiscua ac vilia mercari,: varia promiscaque cogitatio, (al. promiscua): opinionis tam promiscae errores,.—Hence, adv., in three forms.
Form prōmiscam (acc. form from promiscus), in common, indiscriminately, promiscuously (ante-class.): promiscam dicebant pro promiscue, Paul. ex Müll.: ut meā laetitiā laetus promiscam siet,: cetera promiscam voluit communia haberi, Varr. ap. .—
Form prōmiscē, in common, indiscriminately, indifferently (post-class.), B. and K.; ; Weissenb.: indistincte atque promisce annotare, Gell. praef. § 2; 7, 3, 52: promisce atque indefinite largiri,: verbo uti,.—
Form prōmiscŭē (the class. form), in common, promiscuously: (mares et feminae) promiscue in fluminibus perluuntur, * : promiscue puberes atque negotiatores interficere,: promiscue toto quam proprie parvā frui parte (Campi Martii) malletis,; ; ;

promulgo
